title: NoiseXcape
team: Andrea Cutroni, Elena Corio, Symon Kipekemi, Giovanni Carlo Volpe
description: Predicting urban noise levels from open spatial data alone, benchmarking machine-learning models against costly traditional noise mapping.
body: NoiseXcape tests whether urban noise can be predicted from open spatial data instead of costly traditional mapping campaigns. Eighteen features — land use, road proximity, and space-syntax centralities among them — were extracted from OpenStreetMap for Barcelona to train a set of shallow learning models and an artificial neural network, with PCA reducing feature dimensionality and SHAP providing model interpretability.

Tree-based models outperformed linear ones, with Random Forest achieving the best regression and classification results. Cross-city testing showed that transferability is sensitive to demographic differences between cities, though relative noise gradients held up well across contexts.

sections.title: Noise Data
body: Barcelona’s measured noise map, projected onto the OSM road network — every segment carrying the level recorded within ten metres of it, for day, evening and night. This is what the models are asked to reproduce from spatial data alone, and what an equivalent map would otherwise cost a survey to produce.

The distribution shifts rather than shrinks after dark: the city loses its loudest streets but gains a mass of segments in the 45–55 dB range, so the night model is predicting a different problem, not a quieter version of the same one.

sections.title: Workflow
body: Four open datasets go in and a trained predictor comes out. Each source is preprocessed onto the same road segments, assembled into an 18-feature table, explored and reduced, then used to train shallow models and a neural network — with an ablation study and SHAP feeding back into training rather than only reporting on it.

sections.title: Feature Exploration
body: Eighteen features per road segment, in five families: what the road is, how the network uses it, where movement stops and starts, and what surrounds it. Each is mapped across the whole city, and each carries the reason it should predict noise at all.

scenes.title: Road
scenes.caption: Road category and total building-to-building width — the structural predictors, standing in for traffic capacity, speed and how far sound carries.

scenes.title: Centrality
scenes.caption: Betweenness accumulates through-traffic; straightness marks the streets that carry it fast and continuously.

scenes.title: Closeness
scenes.caption: Global closeness finds the centre that attracts movement; the 400 m radius finds local circulation, and with it fine-grained variation.

scenes.title: Points
scenes.caption: Traffic signals, transport stops and points of interest within 50 m — the locations that force stop-and-go movement.

scenes.title: Land Use
scenes.caption: Green, industrial and commercial share within 50 m. Green cover is the one feature that consistently pushes the prediction down.

sections.title: Dimensionality Reduction
body: Most of the eighteen features correlate only moderately with each other, which is encouraging for modelling but leaves little for principal component analysis to compress. The elbow sits at PC2, but explained variance only flattens to nothing around PC16 — so most of the set is doing some work, and little can be discarded outright.

sections.title: Regression & Classification
body: Predicting the decibel value directly, then predicting which band it falls in. Tree-based models beat the linear one decisively — Random Forest reaches R² 0.705 on held-out data against linear regression’s 0.446 — and the gap between train and test scores shows how much of that comes from memorising the training city. The neural network converges but does not overtake them.

sections.title: SHAP Analysis
body: What the model is actually using. Across the whole test set, traffic signals and global closeness dominate, with betweenness and straightness behind them — the movement features outweigh the physical description of the street. The waterfall plots take single segments the model got worst and show which feature pushed each prediction away from the truth.
